newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey tenders for first nuclear plant, sees more.
newsitem.headline: Turkey tenders for first nuclear plant, sees more.

text.p: Turkey announced an international tender on Tuesday for its first nuclear power plant and said more were urgently needed to catch up with rising power demand.
"Turkey will face serious energy shortages in the years to come unless it takes dramatic measures. The nuclear power plant is the most serious of such measures," said Energy Minister Recai Kutan.

"There will be more of such plants after work for the first one gets underway," he told a briefing arranged by the state power utility company TEAS on plans for the nuclear power plant, which Turkey has been considering for the past three decades.
Brushing aside criticism from environmentalists, local residents and some politicians, TEAS announced terms for the nuclear plant tender and said it would collect bids by June 30, 1997.
The plant is to be located near Akkuyu village on the Mediterranean.
"Well reputed and qualified companies are invited to submit sealed bids for furnishing of Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant," TEAS said. It said there were two options.

The first was a plant that would have one or more units with a capacity ranging from 900 MegaWatts (MW) to 1,400 MW. The other option's range was between 2,400 MW to 2,800 MW. Each power production unit in both options should have a capacity of 600 MW or more, according to the terms of the tender.
TEAS said the plant would be fully financed by the builder on a turn-key basis.
"The plant will cost about $1.5 to $2 billion depending on the option chosen," TEAS general manager Afif Demirkiran told Reuters during the briefing.
The tender terms specified that the only companies to be considered would be those which have previously built at least two such plants without accidents, he said.
He said the following companies and groups qualified for the project according to the preliminary studies and were expected to show interest in the tender:
ABB-Atom, ABB-Combustion Engineering, General Electric, General Electric-Hitachi, Toshiba, Westinghouse, Framatome of France, KWU-Siemens, NPI, AECL of Canada and Mitsubishi Elec..
"The first unit is planned to go on stream in December 2005. The other units will become operational the following year," Demirkiran said.
He said the plant, which will produce about 11 billion kiloWatt-hours (kWh) a year when running at capacity, will have an operational lifetime of 40 years from the beginning of production.
He said the plant would use annually 25 tonnes of enriched uranium or 125 tonnes of natural uranium, depending on the type of nuclear power production which is chosen.
Demirkiran said Turkey had uranium reserves of 9,000 tonnes but importing uranium would be cheaper than producing locally.

The tender allows companies to design the cooling system -- the core of a nuclear power plant -- from among types including pressurised heavy water reactors, boiling water reactors, or pressurised water reactors.
Radioactive waste from the fuel will be stored in pools at the plant site for 20 years, which could be extended to 40 years later, Demirkiran said.
The winner of the tender will have to train personnel and provide fuel for the first seven years of operation, he said.

Turkey's power production will be about 93.1 billion kWh this year against a demand of 97.5 billion kWh. The difference has been bridged by electricity imports from Iran since August and Bulgaria since last week.
"From now on, every two or three years we have to tender for another nuclear plant," he said.
He said Turkey might consider a second nuclear plant near the town of Sinop on the Black Sea coast.
--Ankara Newsroom, 90-312-4462940
